summary: Provides the test plan and results supporting advancement of RFC 2679, the one-way delay metric, along the Standards Track following the process in RFC 6576. It focuses on the metric definitions instead of implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the IETF makes a measurement method a formal standard, it usually asks whether two independent tools that follow the same written rules produce the same answers. RFC 6808 is that test for one-way delay, the time a packet takes to travel in a single direction. Two tools were put on the same network path, their results were compared statistically, and the answer was that they agree well enough for the specification to be called unambiguous.

subtitle: The test plan and results that were used to argue that the one-way delay metric should become a standard.

tldr.problem: The IETF wanted the one-way delay metric in RFC 2679 to become a formal Internet Standard, but the usual test of protocol interoperability does not fit a metric, which is a definition rather than a protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts two independent measurement tools on the same path, checks that they produce statistically indistinguishable delay distributions, and fixes the limits that decide equivalence before the comparison is run.
tldr.outcome: The results support advancing RFC 2679 with small revisions, and the revised text was left for later work. The document also found that the inverse percentile was implemented by neither tool, which makes it a candidate for removal.

today: RFC 6808 is an Informational RFC published in December 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents the evidence for advancing RFC 2679 and says that the revised text of that RFC was left for future action.

sections.title: A Different Way to Advance a Standard
sections.content:
The IETF's IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group has wanted its metrics to move along the Standards Track since 2001. The usual route for a protocol is to test that independent implementations interoperate, but that route did not fit a metric. It proved hard to reach agreement on how to compare implementations, because many legitimate sources of variation survive any attempt to keep the network paths equal, and because the definitions allow considerable variation in their parameters. Flexibility in a metric definition is essential for customisation and broad appeal, and it is exactly what made the comparison task hard.

The process the RFC follows comes from RFC 6576, and its first principle is that the metric definitions, not the implementations, are the objects being evaluated. Equivalent test results are the evidence that a metric specification is clear and unambiguous. This is the metric equivalent of protocol interoperability: the process either gives confidence that the wording is clear, or shows where the wording should be revised.

The working group also agreed that the test plan should contain the threshold for deciding equivalence, settled before the cross-implementation comparisons begin, and that the plan should include same-implementation comparisons to inform that threshold. The RFC therefore supplies the documentation that accompanies the protocol action request for RFC 2679: the test setup, the results for each implementation, an evaluation of each specification clause, and the conclusions.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols are usually made standard by checking that two independent implementations can talk to each other. A measurement method is not a protocol, so this RFC uses a different test: if two separate tools, following the same written rules, produce the same numbers, the rules must be unambiguous.

sections.title: How the Test Path Was Built
sections.content:
The two implementations were NetProbe version 5.8.5, an earlier version of the tool used in AT&T's IP network performance measurement system, and Perfas+ version 3.1, developed by Deutsche Telekom. NetProbe sends UDP packets of variable size and can produce test streams with Periodic or Poisson sample distributions. Perfas+ also uses UDP unicast packets of variable size, and supports Periodic, Poisson or uniform distributions.

The test path runs over the Internet between two sites, carried inside a Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol version 3 (L2TPv3) tunnel. The tunnel headers conceal the test equipment addresses and ports from the hash functions that would otherwise spread different test streams across parallel network resources and so vary their performance. At each end, a pair of VLANs inside the tunnel is looped back, so a test stream crosses the tunnel twice but looks like a one-way test to the equipment. A network emulator on a Fedora 14 Linux host, using the netem tool in the Fedora 2.6.35.11 kernel, injected delay on one interface; the links around it turned out to be 100baseTx-HD when testing finished, which was not intended and probably added a small amount of delay variation.

Each test used common packet rates of 1 and 10 packets per second with Poisson or Periodic distributions, and IP packet sizes of 64, 340 and 500 bytes. Those sizes cover a reasonable range while avoiding fragmentation, and they match the notion of standard formed packets in Section 15 of RFC 2330. Every test sent a stream of at least 300 packets from source to destination, with Periodic streams at 1 second spacing.
sections.plainLanguage: The two tools were put on the same path across the internet, hidden inside a tunnel so that the network would treat their traffic the same way. A software device on the network added controlled delays, and both tools sent packets of 64, 340 and 500 bytes so that the results could be compared.

sections.title: How Wrong the Clocks Could Be
sections.content:
Measuring one-way delay needs two clocks that agree, and each implementation has to report how far its own clock might be wrong. RFC 2679 gives the formula: the total time-varying uncertainty is the clock synchronisation uncertainty plus the resolution of the source clock and of the destination clock, and the total wire-time uncertainty is the sum of the source and destination host-time to wire-time bounds. A third test, over small packets and an isolated minimal network, estimates the systematic and random parts of those errors. In a run of hundreds of singletons the median is the systematic error, and what is left after subtracting the median is the random error.

NetProbe works above the UDP layer, using host time rather than the wire time preferred by RFC 2330, and its accuracy is usually limited by NTP synchronisation, typically taken as about +/-1 ms of error. Its reported resolution in the version tested was 1 microsecond, which contributes at least +/-1 microsecond of error. Calibrating over a cross-connect cable with 64-byte packets, 300 singletons over 30 seconds, put the systematic error as high as 110 microseconds, with the random error range on the order of 116 microseconds.

Perfas+ was configured to use GPS synchronisation, with NTP as a fall-back, and its time stamp accuracy is typically 0.1 ms. Its reported resolution was also 1 microsecond. Its own calibration put the systematic error as high as 323 microseconds, with the random error range below 232 microseconds. Perfas+ does not support traceroute, which meant the measured path had to be traced from one of the tunnel-head routers.
sections.plainLanguage: A delay measurement is only as good as the clocks at each end, so each tool had to say how wrong its clock might be. NetProbe's clock came out closer to true than Perfas+'s, and both tools reported their results to the nearest microsecond.

sections.title: The Limits Set Before Comparing
sections.content:
The thresholds that decide equivalence were fixed in advance. The point of them is modest: the allowable errors, corrections and confidence levels only have to be enough to catch a misinterpretation of the specification that leads two implementations to diverge. They also have to be enough to compensate for differences in the measured path, because it was simply not possible to measure fully identical paths in the VLAN loopback configuration used.

For the Anderson-Darling K-sample comparisons, the required confidence factor for the cross-implementation comparisons must be the smallest of two values: a 0.95 confidence factor at 1 millisecond resolution, or the smallest confidence factor, together with its resolution, of the two same-implementation comparisons for the same test conditions. Two corrections are allowed before the comparison is run: a constant time accuracy error of as much as +/-0.5 ms may be removed from one implementation's distribution, and a constant propagation delay error of as much as +2 ms, caused by using different subnets between the switch and the measurement device at each site, may also be removed. The same limits apply to comparisons involving the mean of a sample or other central statistics.

The working group's judgement was that these numbers are tight enough to expose a real divergence without being so tight that ordinary measurement noise trips them. The RFC notes that RFC 2679 contains only five instances of the requirement term MUST outside the boilerplate, so the number of clauses that actually needed testing was small.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the results were compared, the RFC fixed how close the two sets of numbers had to be to count as a match: a 95 per cent confidence factor at millisecond resolution, plus two allowances for known clock and cabling offsets.

sections.title: The Tests and What They Showed
sections.content:
The main test compared the delay distributions from the two implementations with the Anderson-Darling K-sample test, using 64-octet IP packets sampled once per second for 300 seconds, with the emulator set to 100 ms of average delay and +/-50 ms of uniform variation. NetProbe had one same-implementation pair that failed the criterion, and the RFC notes that this pair travelled the path in opposite directions, which points at live network effects rather than the tools. Every Perfas+ pair passed. The cross-implementation comparison passed too, with a combined statistic of 0.85537 and a P-value of 0.17967, so both tools' results were consistent with coming from a common distribution. The conclusion drawn was that the two implementations are capable of producing equivalent one-way delay distributions from their reading of RFC 2679. A follow-up experiment found that with no emulated delay variation at all no comparison passed, while a variation of +/-2.5 ms was enough for the adjusted samples to pass.

Three further tests checked specific clauses. On the loss threshold, with the threshold set to 3 seconds, NetProbe marked every packet delayed by more than 3 seconds as lost, which gave 342 lost packets in one stream; Perfas+ uses a fixed threshold of about a minute, but applying the 3 second threshold afterwards would have given 195 lost packets. The RFC takes the view that this post-processing assumption is compliant and that RFC 2679 should be revised slightly to say so. On the first-bit-to-last-bit convention, the delay increase between 64-byte and 500-byte packets was typically 1.1 to 1.5 ms, which implies a link of about 3 Mbit/s on the path, while the lowest speed link was found to be about 45 Mbit/s and should have given roughly 0.077 ms. On the difference sample metric, with the path delay raised by 1000 ms, NetProbe measured the increase with a 182 microsecond error and Perfas+ with a 7 microsecond error.

The last test checked which summary statistics the tools implement. Both implement the minimum, NetProbe alone implements the percentile and the median, and neither implements the inverse percentile. Since only that one statistic is ignored by both, the RFC identifies it as a candidate for removal or deprecation in a revision, noting that this small discrepancy does not affect the case for advancement.
sections.plainLanguage: The two tools' delay results could not be told apart by a statistical test, which is the result the RFC needed. The other tests checked particular rules in the specification, found one that should be worded more clearly, and found one statistic that neither tool implements.

sections.title: Conclusions, Errata and Security
sections.content:
The results support the advancement of RFC 2679 to the next step of the Standards Track, because its requirements are judged to be clear and unambiguous once evaluated against two implementations that produced statistically equivalent results under conditions configured to be as close to identical as possible. The RFC also points to areas where minor revisions are warranted, and to the IETF guidance on reporting metrics in RFC 6703, which a revision should refer to. There was one erratum against RFC 2679 with the status Held for Document Update, and the RFC notes that the authors of a revision should review all errata filed by then rather than rely on this document. The revised text of RFC 2679 was not yet ready for review, so approving a revision was left for future action.

On security, the RFC says that the considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks are relevant here as well, and points to RFC 4656 and RFC 5357. That is the whole of the security section: this is a test report, and it inherits the exposure of any tool that sends measurement traffic across a live network.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC concludes that the one-way delay specification can move forward as a standard, with a few small wording changes to be made later. It notes that measuring a live network carries the usual risks of any active measurement tool.

items.title: Confidence factor
items.text: 0.95 at 1 ms resolution, or the smaller of the two same-implementation results.

items.title: Time accuracy correction
items.text: Up to +/-0.5 ms may be removed from one distribution.

items.title: Propagation delay correction
items.text: Up to +2 ms may be removed for the cabling difference at each site.

items.title: What it is for
items.text: Enough to catch a divergence, not so tight that ordinary noise trips it.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TESTS AND WHAT EACH CHECKED

items.title: Delay distributions
items.text: Do the two tools produce results from a common distribution?

items.title: Loss threshold
items.text: Do both mark packets delayed beyond the threshold as lost?

items.title: First bit to last bit
items.text: Does the delay grow as the packet gets bigger, as the convention requires?

items.title: Difference sample
items.text: Do both measure the same increase when the path delay is changed?
